msg: raw() turns the value into HTML and skips escaping - a stored '<script>' in that value runs in every visitor's browser. Drop raw() (<%= value %> escapes by default) or use sanitize(value, tags: %w[b i a]).
#html_safe marks the string as already-escaped, so ERB prints it verbatim. Remove .html_safe, or build the markup with tag helpers (content_tag/safe_join) so only the literal parts are trusted.
<%== is the shorthand for <%= raw - identical unescaped output with no visible 'raw' to grep for. Change it to <%= and escape explicitly where you really need HTML.
render inline: compiles the string as an ERB template; user text reaching it is server-side template injection, not just XSS. Render a real template file and pass the value as a local.
ERB's HTML escaping does not make a value safe inside a <script> block - quotes and </script> both break out. Wrap it: <%= j(value) %> (escape_javascript) for a JS string.

to_json inside <script> leaves '</script>' and '<!--' intact, so one string field closes your script tag. Use <%= json_escape(value.to_json) %>, or move the data to a data- attribute and JSON.parse it.

A URL taken straight from a record can start with 'javascript:' or 'data:', which fires on click even though the attribute was HTML-escaped. Pass it through a route helper, or check the scheme against an http/https allowlist first.

link_to with a params[] destination is an open redirect and a javascript:-URL sink - the attacker supplies the query string. Redirect through a named route, or validate the value against a list of allowed paths.

An on* attribute is a JavaScript context: HTML escaping still leaves the value executable once the browser decodes the entity. Move the handler to a Stimulus controller or an addEventListener and pass the value in a data- attribute.
An unquoted attribute value ends at the first space, so a value containing a space can add attributes such as onerror=. Quote it: attr="<%= value %>".
The fourth argument of content_tag is 'escape'; passing false prints the body as HTML. Leave it at true and pass already-built tag helpers as the body instead.

sanitize() without a tags: allowlist falls back to Rails' default list, which is wider than most views need and changes between releases. State the allowlist: sanitize(value, tags: %w[b i em a], attributes: %w[href]).

simple_format(..., sanitize: false) keeps every tag in the text and only adds paragraphs around it. Remove the option, or sanitize the value yourself with an explicit tags: allowlist before formatting.

A value interpolated into a <style> block lands in a CSS context, where url(...) and expression-like payloads survive HTML escaping. Set the value as an inline style attribute on the element, or expose it as a CSS custom property you control.

A policy carrying 'unsafe-inline' for script-src removes the browser's last line of defence against exactly the injections above. Move inline scripts into asset files and use the nonce Rails' content_security_policy generator provides.
